articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_zh: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order , external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
By GREG HEFFER, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:03 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 12:39 EDT, 29 September 2026
Andy Burnham today vowed to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections.
In his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham promised to introduce a 'new politics' through electoral reform.
He confirmed he would fight the next General Election, scheduled for 2029, with a Labour manifesto commitment to alter the system for choosing UK governments.
The PM, a long-time supporter of proportional representation, said a change would ensure 'everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard'.
Mr Burnham announced the creation of a new 'national commission' for electoral reform and invited rival political parties to be part of its work.
Changing the first-past-the-post system to proportional representation could allow smaller parties – including the Greens – to form part of a Westminster government.
Mr Burnham's plans are likely to revive warnings of a 'coalition of chaos' – made up of a variety of Left-wing or nationalist parties – taking charge of Britain.
But in his conference speech in Liverpool, the PM suggested it was the current first-past-the-post system that was to blame for the country's recent churn of premiers.
Andy Burnham today set out his intent to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections
He argued that Britain should not be governed by a 'divisive' administration elected with '30 per cent of the vote or less'.
Just ten weeks on from his brutal ousting of Sir Keir Starmer as PM, Mr Burnham told Labour members there was a need to change the country's politics.
He said: 'Westminster prizes point-scoring over problem-solving. And that is why so many things go unfixed for so long.
'If we want to change Britain, we need to change ourselves. I will work as hard as I can to get as much cross-party support for our plan for Britain as I can.
'If we can secure that, it will project a message of confidence and stability to the markets and the world about Britain's future direction.'
The PM has so far refused to call a snap General Election in order to win his own mandate from the country.
This is despite him having called for the Tories to do exactly that when they changed leaders while in power.
But he used his first Labour conference speech as PM to demand a 'new politics', as he bowed to calls from his party's MPs for a national commission on electoral reform.
Mr Burnham added: 'We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times.
'It is always in my mind that I'm the seventh PM in ten years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
'We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No10 to a divisive government on 30 per cent of the vote or less.
'Conference, in past years you have voted twice to support electoral reform.
'I hear you, I agree with you and today I am announcing a new national commission on electoral reform.
'I invite all political parties to be a part of its work.
'We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard.'
However, immediately after Mr Burnham's speech, senior Labour figures questioned his desire to pursue a change to the UK's voting system.
Asked if there were any elements of the speech she may not have agreed on, skills minister Jacqui Smith, said: 'Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities.
'Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested with what it comes out with.
'But you know, respect to Andy, he has also long argued for that – it is something that has got a lot of support in the hall, probably a considerable amount of support in the country, and fair enough to him for trying to find a way through it.'
Former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn described Mr Burnham's address as an 'inspirational speech' but also suggested he was unsure about electoral reform.
'We'll see what the commission on electoral reform produces,' he said.
Labour's party conference voted to support moving towards a proportional representation voting system in 2022.
But the party's 2024 manifesto instead focused its electoral and constitutional changes on extending voting to 16 and 17-year-olds and House of Lords reform.
Mr Burnham has previously spoken of how his late father Roy – who died earlier this month after suffering with Alzheimer's – was unaware that his son had swung behind one of his political passions, a change in the voting system to proportional representation.
'I don't think he's ever realised, because of his condition, that I've come round to PR, which is one of his missions – to get me to accept that,' the PM told The Times in July.

articles.title_zh: OpenAI DevDay recap: AI lab rolls out Dots agents, Altman and Friar comment on IPO
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI held its annual DevDay developer conference on Tuesday, where the artificial intelligence company announced a flurry of new products and features .
This year's DevDay comes as OpenAI has been under intense pressure to address mounting safety concerns after it disclosed several incidents where its models behaved in unintended ways, and the startup held back its latest Astra model over safety concerns.
Earlier this month, the company endorsed a call to slow down the pace of advanced AI model development in order to better address the technology's risks.
CNBC's reporters are covering the OpenAI DevDay event live from San Francisco, and remotely from Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey.
Friar said OpenAI wants to IPO "when the time is right for our business," echoing Altman's earlier comments to CNBC. She said an IPO is "not a destination," but a "milestone on the journey" and "another type of fundraising."
"I think Sam is correct in saying we don't want to get distracted by suddenly being a public company in the midst of really making sure we drive home for customers our focus on safety and alignment," Friar said.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar touted the company's latest price drop on their GPT-6.1 Sol model, and went deeper into the feedback OpenAI's been getting on their higher pricing tiers.
"When we launched our $200 SKU, people thought we'd lost our minds, [that] no one's ever going to spend that per month," Friar told CNBC's Kate Rooney in an interview.
"What we see is not only are people willing to spend more, they're actually moving more towards consumption in consumer, so not just seat-based pricing, but actually saying, 'I need to consume even more credits because I'm getting this great outcome for maybe my small business,'" she added.
Friar said OpenAI has had an "incredible" third quarter. She confirmed CNBC's earlier reporting that the company has seen 70% quarter over quarter growth, and that its enterprise business has doubled since July.
She added that OpenAI's consumer business has benefitted from a number of factors, including better models, images, voice, and the back to school and work period in the U.S. and around the world.
"People are starting to see us show up the ways they need us to show up," Friar said.
Friar declined to comment on whether OpenAI is engaging in early-stage fundraising discussions with investors, as CNBC reported earlier on Tuesday. She emphasized that OpenAI raised $122 billion in March, and said that the company is "very well capitalized."
"My job as a CFO is always to make sure we're making the right decisions on when we take in more capital and then how we deploy that capital," Friar said.
Friar said OpenAI is being more vocal about safety because of what has been happening "out there in the world." But she noted that while there are instances where OpenAI will hold back, there are also instances where the company will continue to "show model progression."
"When we have to pace the frontier, we'll do that," Friar said. "That's what we're showing right now."

articles.title_orig: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers
articles.title_zh: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."
Trump and the CEOs said they had signed an "Accord on Super Intelligence" that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."
Some executives on hand said the accord would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.
Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.
"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."
Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.
The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.
"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.
The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart . The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.
After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.
Other notable guests included Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) president Greg Brockman, Palantir ( PLTR ) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon ( AMZN ) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.
The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.
And in Florida, the attorney general unveiled a new state-level challenge asking a court to halt OpenAI's training of new models unless it puts outside safeguards in place.
But that skepticism didn't change the tenor of the gathering in Washington.
Trump repeatedly brushed off worries about the technology, saying after the meeting that he believes AI will make the world a safer place and that fears about data centers driving up costs were overblown.
He said instead that these new facilities "are going to make communities very happy."
At an event earlier in the day to launch a new government website powered by AI, Trump promised that AI is "going to mostly be put to great use and we'll stop the bad use," through the Department of Justice and FBI.
He added he would "never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."

articles.title_orig: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.title_zh: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan’s plan to open a second trade office in the Philippines is an example of Manila and Taipei accelerating cooperation in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
During a radio interview on Sept. 15, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said that Taipei’s plan to open a second representative office in Cebu, the Philippines’ second largest city, was going smoothly.
Taipei’s trade offices serve as de facto embassies and consulates in countries that officially recognize China, but maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be a rogue province.
Foreign Minister Lin said that the additional trade office would serve travelers and businesses in the central Philippines, and would be an integral part of a proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor.
Days later, Taiwan confirmed that it had donated a decommissioned patrol vessel to the Philippines for use in its coast guard.
These developments are directly related to Beijing’s hostile tactics in the South China Sea, Ray Powell, executive director of Stanford University’s SeaLight maritime transparency project, told RFA. Beijing claims the entirety of the sea as its territory, including the area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.
“Of course China’s aggression in the West Philippine Sea is a central part of this story,” said Powell. “It has made Manila less willing to grant Beijing the kind of deference that other countries like Malaysia or Papua New Guinea have recently been so eager to show on Taiwan policy.”
Papua New Guinea announced in July that it would close the Taiwan trade office in Port Moresby, and Malaysia’s Prime Minister Ibrahim Anwar in August controversially stated in an interview with Al Jazeera that he sees “Taiwan as part of China, period.”
The trend of smaller countries showing deference to China “has conditioned Beijing to expect that its coercive methods will always produce compliance eventually,” Powell said. “For now at least it has not produced that kind of result in the Philippines.”
As a condition of entering into official relations with China, countries must affirm that there is one China and recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China.
China’s official stance, the one-China principle, states that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Many countries maintain their own one-China policies that stop short of the principle to allow unofficial ties with Taipei.
When Taiwan announced the plan to open a new trade office in Cebu, Beijing protested, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urging the Philippines to uphold the one-China Principle through “concrete actions” and refrain from taking steps that could damage relations with China.
“No matter how the DPP authorities collude with external forces or in what form they seek so-called ‘diplomatic breakthroughs,’ their efforts to serve the goal of ‘Taiwan independence’ are doomed to be futile,” Guo said, referring to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party.
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs responded that Manila’s one-China policy remained unchanged but did not prevent economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. was more direct, telling local media: “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them.”
The exchange highlights a widening difference between Manila and Beijing over what the Philippines’ one-China policy allows.
The Taiwan trade office in Cebu should not be interpreted as a change in Manila’s formal position, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Rather, I think it reflects the ongoing expansion and institutionalization of the Philippines’ unofficial and functional relationship with Taiwan,” he said. “This distinction is important: Manila continues to recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China under its one-China Policy, yet it does not view this policy as precluding economic, cultural, or other practical forms of engagement with Taiwan.”
That relationship had already begun expanding before the latest dispute.
In April 2025, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration relaxed decades-old restrictions on engagement with Taiwan. Most Philippine officials may now travel there for economic, trade and investment purposes if they use ordinary passports and do not use their official titles.
The restrictions continue to apply to the president, vice president, foreign secretary and defense secretary, illustrating the line Manila is trying to maintain between functional engagement and steps that might resemble formal diplomatic recognition.
“Currently, Manila appears intent on maintaining a distinction between expanding functional ties and taking actions that could be construed as formal diplomatic recognition,” Kristanto said. “The 2025 guidelines are particularly illustrative: they facilitate interactions with Taiwan for economic and investment purposes while retaining restrictions on contacts involving the Philippines’ most senior officials.”
Practical interests are also driving the relationship. More than 200,000 Filipinos work in Taiwan, and the two sides offer visa-free entry to each other’s citizens. Taipei has also placed greater emphasis on trade, investment, tourism and supply-chain cooperation with the Philippines.
Foreign Minister Lin said the proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor would connect with the U.S.-Japan-Philippines-backed Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative aimed at strengthening infrastructure and supply chains.
Kristanto cautioned against explaining the closer relationship entirely through the South China Sea dispute.
“The deterioration in Manila-Beijing relations has certainly made Taiwan more strategically relevant to the Philippines, and we have seen indications of expanding practical cooperation in areas such as maritime security,” he said.
“But many drivers of closer Philippines-Taiwan relations – economic links, labor, geographical proximity, and supply-chain cooperation – exist independently of the South China Sea dispute. I therefore see pressure from China more as an accelerant to an existing trend than as its sole cause.”
Powell said the Philippines increasingly viewed China’s treatment of Taiwan as part of a wider effort to pressure smaller countries that resisted Beijing’s preferred regional order.
“There’s an active attempt by China, very obvious now, to make a more Sinocentric world and to put down others who do not agree with them – particularly when these others are smaller countries,” Powell said, quoting from a recent SeaLight podcast interview with Teodoro.
Kristanto said the significance of the Cebu office lay less in the facility itself than in Manila’s growing confidence in defining its relationship with Taipei on its own terms.
“Manila appears increasingly willing to insist that maintaining a one-China policy does not give Beijing a veto over its unofficial relationship with Taiwan,” Kristanto said.
“So, in my view, the significance of the Cebu office lies less in the office itself than in what it tells us about how much more comfortable Manila has become in expanding ties with Taiwan while arguing that its formal diplomatic position remains unchanged.”

articles.title_orig: Riley's homer rallies Braves past Phillies in wild-card opener
articles.title_zh: Riley's homer rallies Braves past Phillies in wild-card opener
articles.content_orig:
The Phillies lost to the Braves , 5-3, in Game 1 of the best-of-three Wild Card Series Tuesday afternoon in Atlanta. The Phillies took a 3-2 lead in the top of the seventh inning on a two-RBI triple from catcher J.T. Realmuto before manager Don Mattingly decided to hand the ball over to his closer, Jhoan Duran .
Duran was one of the best closers in baseball in the regular season, but seeing him enter the game in the seventh inning was still a surprising move. He hadn't worked in the seventh inning all season and only did twice (once in the regular season, once in the playoffs) last year. He's generally a ninth-inning-only closer but has gotten some four-out saves.
In this situation, the Braves had the top of the order coming up in the top of the seventh (it was 9-1-2 to start).
"We talked about it before the game: if we were at the top, we were getting to the top, go seventh, eighth (innings)," Mattingly said after the game.
Duran only threw 11 pitches in the seventh inning, then got two outs in the bottom of the eighth before a weak tapper from Michael Harris II turned into an infield single. Duran then hit Ozzie Albies with a pitch before Austin Riley hit a three-run home run. That 3-2 lead turned into a 5-3 deficit that would hold for a final score.
There's an argument that Duran should've been removed before Riley hit, given that the closer was up over 20 pitches at this point -- but there were two outs and he's the best reliever the Phillies have. The Harris hit was only 85.5 mph, just a bouncer that was placed perfectly in the infield.
Mattingly noted after the game that had Duran gotten through the seventh and eighth with a tidy pitch count, he'd have checked with his closer and possibly sent him back out for the ninth. It was a case where the Phillies were trying to use their best and see how deep he could get.
Had the Phillies used a lesser reliever and blown the game, there would've been questions about why one of the top relievers on the planet was sitting in the bullpen unused. Instead of managing to the save stat, Mattingly put his best guy in position to get the game to the ninth with the lead intact. The next question would be who was going to get the ninth inning. If you don't get there with the lead, it doesn't much matter. Saving the best reliever often backfires in the postseason. We've famously seen shots of stud closers like Zach Britton and Craig Kimbrel helplessly watching as their team blew the lead. This time around, Mattingly and the Phillies made the right call. It just didn't work out.
"It's frustrating," Mattingly said. "But in our minds, we had our best guy out there. You live with this one."
Sometimes even the best plans backfire.

articles.title_orig: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.title_zh: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.content_orig:
His slam dunk was a brick.
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., accused former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday of committing perjury when he denied having attended a specific Atlanta Hawks basketball game in 2024 — to Smith’s apparent confusion.
The attempted trick play happened during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Smith’s now-scuttled investigations into President Donald Trump. But it soon emerged that Schmitt had the wrong team.
“Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on Feb. 3, 2024?” Schmitt asked.
“What city would that be in?” a confused-looking Smith replied.
“Atlanta,” Schmitt responded.
Schmitt pressed him again about whether he was in Atlanta on that date and then said he’d give him some “context” — it was the day after Fani Willis , the district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia, “came clean” about her romantic relationship with a prosecutor in her then-pending criminal case against Trump.
“The next day were you in Atlanta?” Schmitt continued.
“I do not believe so,” Smith responded. “I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”
Schmitt then asked whether he ever met with the local prosecutors in Atlanta who charged Trump. “No,” Smith said.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta, at a Warrior-Hawks game, on Feb. 3, 2024, the day after Willis and [Nathan] Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt continued as a staffer held up a poster board that had three text messages about Smith’s going to an event.
The staffer quickly took the poster down as Smith looked on, appearing confused.
“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Schmitt said.
Smith complained that it had been taken down too quickly and that he hadn’t gotten to look at it. “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” Schmitt told him, adding later that he’d go down in history as “a total dirtbag.”
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who was next in line to question Smith, gave him an opportunity to further respond to Schmitt’s attack.
Smith said the only game he remembered going to around that time was a University of Maryland basketball game against the Iowa Hawkeyes featuring star player Caitlin Clark. “The Marshals Service was there with me. You could check if that was the exact date,” Smith said.
Klobuchar then checked the date of the Maryland-Iowa game.
“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93-85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over, scored 30 points,” and the game was in Maryland, she said.
She also chided Schmitt for appearing to mix up the Hawks and the Hawkeyes.
“I would just say for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said.
Schmitt didn’t apologize. Asked by NBC News afterward whether he still thought Smith had perjured himself, he said: “We’ll find out. That’s going to be up to a prosecutor to determine. My job here today was to ask questions and get answers.”
Despite the flub, some right-wing commentators and outlets praised Schmitt for the exchange. Pro-Trump influencer Benny Johnson posted on X that Schmitt “CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself” and “pulled out the receipts.” The post appeared to have been taken down by the late afternoon.
Schmitt later went on “ The Charlie Kirk Show ,” where one of the hosts praised him for the “great moment.” “Good for you on that,” host Andrew Kolvet said.
“Gotta give you some flowers for that, sir,” he said, saying Smith “sat there acting dumbfounded and completely clueless.”
“It was the only NBA or NCAA men’s game going on at that time in Atlanta. He claimed later that he was at another game,” Schmitt responded. “Here’s the thing — my job is to ask the questions. If that’s what his answer is, that’s what his answer is.”
On Tuesday night, Schmitt wrote in a post on X , “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”
Rebecca Shabad is a politics reporter for NBC News based in Washington.
Julie Tsirkin is a correspondent covering Capitol Hill and the White House.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is on top of Wall Street right now, advising on more than $1 trillion in merger deals and generating more than $12 billion in equities revenue in the first six months of the year alone.
Those records make it all the more striking that Goldman's board has reportedly discussed replacing CEO David Solomon, 64, with president John Waldron, 57, as early as next year.
The succession plan, which would elevate Solomon to executive chairman, could be voted on by the bank's board in coming months, The Wall Street Journal reported late Monday.
The transition would be one of the "smoother and more deliberate" leadership handovers seen on Wall Street, Wells Fargo banking analyst Mike Mayo wrote Monday.
But there's a key risk facing Goldman: Solomon may not be ready to give up his seat, and Waldron may not be willing to wait for it indefinitely.
Solomon has gotten Goldman back on track after an ill-fated foray into consumer banking earlier in his tenure. With help from a deals rebound powered by the Trump administration and the artificial intelligence boom, Goldman is once again a clean story for investors: It's the top pure-play investment bank.
"It's just very hard for a person like that to decide they are really going to retire," said retired University of Delaware law professor Charles Elson . "Being 65 years old today is like being 55 was 30 years ago."
Elson also noted that Solomon is chairman of Goldman's board and holds outsized influence over the body, making it hard for him to be forced out.
Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto said there is "no definitive timeline for succession" at the bank. Bank boards often discuss succession planning over the near, medium and longer term.
Another expert in CEO succession, Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, said it would be bad governance if Goldman's board was trying to "drive out a high performing CEO like David Solomon."
Under Solomon, who took over as CEO in 2018, Goldman shares are up more than 300%, the second-best performance versus the KBW Bank Index , according to Mayo. Only JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has led his firm for nearly 21 years, has done better.
That leaves Goldman in something of a bind: Even if Solomon is planning on leaving in a year, he has little incentive to say so. Doing so would make him a lame duck with less influence inside the bank, according to Elson.
But if Solomon decides he wants to remain CEO amid an AI boom that he believes is in its early innings, Waldron may tire of waiting for the crown.
After all, Waldron, Goldman's president and chief operating officer, had reportedly been in discussions for leadership roles at alternative asset managers Apollo and Carlyle .
To keep him, Goldman gave Waldron an $80 million retention package that lasts through 2030. Even then, a deep-pocketed suitor could make a play for Waldron, said Elson.
"There will always be tension in a set up like that," Elson said. "It's like Prince Charles waiting for his mother to die. You can't set your own priorities, because there's someone else in charge."

articles.title_zh: Presley Gerber’s Sober Team Reportedly Warned Facility He Was ‘High’ Before It Agreed to Take Him Alternative Headline
articles.content_orig:
Presley Gerber's sober team reportedly told the Santa Monica residence where he died that he was already "high" before staff agreed to accept him.
Multiple sources, including one described as having direct knowledge, told TMZ that someone working with Presley contacted Resolutions Living on the afternoon of Sept. 19 and asked whether the sober-living residence would take him because he was under the influence. According to the sources, staff told the caller to bring him in.
Presley arrived that evening and reportedly remained under the influence of an unidentified substance. The 27-year-old son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber was found unresponsive the following morning and pronounced dead at 9:45 a.m. on Sept. 20.
Santa Monica police are investigating his death as a suspected overdose, but the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner has not determined an official cause or manner of death. No toxicology results have established what Presley had allegedly taken or whether the decision to admit him contributed to his death.
TMZ's sources said the call to Resolutions Living took place before Presley reached the property. A member of his sober team reportedly explained that they wanted to bring Presley to the residence but first needed to know whether staff would accept him in his current condition.
Staff allegedly agreed. After Presley arrived, sources described him as continuing to appear intoxicated and behaving erratically. The substance he had allegedly taken has not been publicly identified.
Resolutions Living's owner did not respond to TMZ's request for comment about the allegations. The residence has not publicly provided its account of the phone call, what staff were told about Presley's condition or what assessment was conducted when he arrived.
TMZ places Presley's arrival shortly after 6 p.m. on Sept. 19. NBC News , citing a law enforcement source, previously reported that he arrived at approximately 10 p.m.
TMZ separately reported that a friend and a personal coach who was part of Presley's support team brought him to the residence after his team arranged the placement.
Sources told the outlet that Crawford, Rande and Kaia Gerber knew Presley had been struggling and had discussed him returning to treatment, but claimed the family did not know he was going to Resolutions Living. Those details have not been confirmed publicly by the Gerber family.
The California Department of Health Care Services told TMZ that it had no record of Resolutions Living operating as a licensed residential substance-use disorder treatment facility in Santa Monica.
The agency said available information indicated that the property operated as a sober-living environment or recovery residence. Homes in that category do not require the same DHCS license as residential substance-use treatment centers as long as they are not providing services such as detoxification or treatment planning.
Resolutions Living's own website describes the property as a mental-health recovery residence offering a sober-living program, long-term housing and 24/7 on-site staff.
The Los Angeles Times reported that Resolutions Living is not subject to the state oversight applied to licensed treatment facilities because it operates as a recovery residence and does not offer treatment on site. The owners operate a separate licensed mental-health treatment facility, Resolutions Therapeutic Services, about a mile away.
The lack of a residential substance-use treatment license does not by itself establish that Resolutions Living was operating illegally. It does distinguish the residence from a facility licensed to provide medical detoxification or residential addiction treatment.
Nick Mathews, who operates a separate drug-treatment center and is not identified as having treated Presley, told TMZ that someone actively using substances should not be admitted to a sober-living facility that is not equipped or licensed to manage detoxification.
Mathews' comments represent his professional opinion based on the circumstances described to him. There has been no public regulatory finding that Resolutions Living violated a law or medical standard by accepting Presley.
People close to Presley had previously told TMZ that they believed he should have been directed to a medical detox facility when he arrived under the influence. The latest reporting adds the allegation that staff knew about his condition before he reached the property.
Months before his death, Presley had been open about his efforts to address addiction and his mental health.
In March, he shared an Instagram video from Mexico while preparing to undergo ibogaine treatment. Presley said he was frightened about the experience as he prepared for another attempt to address problems he had struggled with for years.
Crawford, Rande and Kaia publicly supported him beneath the post, leaving messages expressing their pride. Presley later appeared with his parents at a mental-health event in Malibu in June, where he discussed addiction, medication and his decision to speak openly about his experiences.
TMZ also cited sources close to Presley who said an unidentified doctor had been giving him ketamine despite his history of problems with the drug. The doctor has not been named, and toxicology results have not determined whether ketamine played any role in Presley's death.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner said responding paramedics pronounced Presley dead at 9:45 a.m. on Sept. 20.
A deputy medical examiner examined his body the following day, but both the cause and manner of death were deferred pending additional testing or studies. The department said deferred cases can take several months before a final determination is made.
Santa Monica police have said they are investigating Presley's death as a suspected overdose and have found no indication of foul play.

articles.title_orig: Trump says tech execs signed ‘morally binding’ accord to help police AI
articles.title_zh: Trump says tech execs signed ‘morally binding’ accord to help police AI
articles.content_orig:
The White House meeting came as some AI leaders issued warnings about AI.
President Donald Trump said that tech leaders he met with at the White House on Tuesday had signed a "constitution" to police themselves amid dire warnings from artificial intelligence leaders about the technology.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said the agreement was voluntary.
The meeting came as AI leaders are issuing warnings about the threat of AI and calling for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans. Following those warnings, lawmakers are weighing what -- if any -- action should be taken.
Along with Johnson and members of Trump's Cabinet, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attended the meeting along with Elon Musk, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang from Nvidia, Palintir's Alex Karp and Shyam Sankar, Amaxzon's Jeff Bezos, and Greg Brockman from OpenAI.
The president indicated before the meeting that he didn't want global collaboration or regulation of the industry and said he discussed it with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House last week.
"We talked about it, not that much because I didn't want to do anything. We're leading, so why would I want to do anything? And, and a lot of people said, 'Let's do it together with China.' But then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know. But we do work with them in so many ways," Trump said.
"We're leading now over China and everyone else and I want to keep it that way. I want to keep it that way," Trump said. "The only way you can keep it that way is to do exactly what we're doing right now. We don't want to stifle growth."
The president repeated that law enforcement would be the key mechanism in stopping companies who "go down a very dark and dangerous path" on AI.
"At the same time, we want people to behave honestly. We want them to be trustworthy, and that's why we have the DOJ. That's why we have the FBI. That's why we have forms of government that are very effective if people decide to go down a very dark and dangerous path," Trump said.
Zuckerberg has pushed back on calls from other tech leaders to collectively slow down AI, saying "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely."
The meeting will also include other tech leaders.
This won't be the first time that top tech leaders have met with Trump on the issue. The Meta CEO also attended the state dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, along with the CEOs of OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, SpaceX and executives from Amazon and Apple. Amodei also had dinner with Trump late on Sunday night.'
The president has said that the warnings about the technology and calls to slow down AI development are a "hoax."
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX[...]," Trump said in a social media post in mid-September, before comparing the warnings to his impeachments.
The president has made clear that he does not believe in regulating the technology. Just last week while addressing the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said the U.S. "rejects" a global attempt to regulate AI.
Johnson told reporters two weeks ago about the meeting, saying there would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play in that."
While Johnson called on the companies to "self-regulate," he also also stressed that the U.S. should not lose its competitive edge in the space.
"We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for," Johnson said.
On Monday, Johnson said the the fears of the threat of AI is a Chinese psychological operation and are politically motivated.
"This is what Democrats do. They glom on to something and say, 'This is doom and gloom and everyone will die if we don't win,'" he told Fox Business. "Don't buy it. It is a Chinese psyop."
The White House has not responded to ABC News when asked about the meeting.

articles.title_orig: Appeals court seems likely to let Boasberg’s contempt probe continue
articles.title_zh: Appeals court seems likely to let Boasberg’s contempt probe continue
articles.content_orig:
A DOJ lawyer surprised judges on the full appeals court in Washington, D.C., by making former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem the "sacrificial lamb" of a judge's contempt inquiry without "any reason to think that she, in particular" willfully violated a court order.
The DOJ's Brett Shumate took the lead for the government at the much-anticipated en banc proceeding at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Tuesday morning.
Several judges suggested that the government, without a "clear and indisputable right" to relief, was not close to securing an "extraordinary" writ of mandamus that would force Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg to shut down an "unlawful, unnecessary, and futile" probe into the "mental state of senior government officials" who defied a March 15, 2025, temporary retraining order (TRO) blocking Alien Enemies Act (AEA) deportations.

After all, a previous en banc panel already allowed the district judge to "require the government to identify the decision makers who directed the potentially contemptuous actions" — the disembarking of AEA deportees in El Salvador.
At stake is the judge-ordered testimony of fired DOJ attorney Erez Reuveni and Deputy Assistant Attorney General Drew Ensign as part of the inquiry.
Reuveni was placed on leave and then fired after nearly 15 years at the DOJ in April 2025 after he said he "refused directions from his superiors to file a brief misrepresenting" facts about Kilmar Abrego Garcia , a Maryland man and Salvadoran national whom courts have deemed to have been wrongly deported and vindictively prosecuted.
Reuveni alleged that Ensign was there the day before Boasberg issued the restraining order the government flouted, when former Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove — President Donald Trump's ex-personal attorney — had suggested during a meeting that the government give the courts a "f— you" if the government was blocked from carrying out mass AEA deportations.
At the time, Bove's nomination for a judgeship at the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals was pending. He went on to be confirmed , and was among the current or former DOJ officials who submitted a "cursory" declaration about his role in advising Noem.
In peppering the DOJ with questions about this, U.S. Circuit Judge Patricia Millett indicated that she thinks the "f— you" episode warrants some more inquiry.
"I think the district court described Secretary Noem as the purported decision-maker, but as Judge Childs just mentioned, the district court doesn't have to accept that as the only relevant decision-maker," she said. "I assume you would agree that the ultimate decision-maker is not the only one who could have been in contempt of court."
"For example, because it is clear from the declarations that she was receiving legal advice from a number of people within the Justice Department. Now, if an attorney providing legal advice to the secretary were to tell the secretary, 'You have the legal authority to expletive the court order on this and go ahead and disembark people. Might it be accurate that that attorney would just as well be in contempt of court as the secretary potentially?" Millett asked.
"I think that's an interesting question that a prosecutor may wish to probe — " the DOJ lawyer began to respond.
"I'm not asking you what prosecutors can look into," Millett cut Shumate off. "I'm asking you whether contempt of court could be committed potentially for court to invest for court to decide whether I need to find show cause as to or find cause as to additional people. Could it include an attorney who advised somebody to expletive the court, and go ahead in the court's order, and go ahead, and disembark people? Would that potentially be contempt of court in the view of the United States?"
"I think it depends on the facts, your honor," Shumate replied.
"Well, then I think the district court needs to ask some more questions," the Barack Obama-appointed jurist summed up.
A short time later, U.S. Circuit Judge Florence Pan, a Joe Biden appointee, referred to Millett's line of questioning and directly referenced the Bove incident without naming him.
"It sounds to me that like you're trying to constrain his discretion to conduct this — it's an investigation as to whether he should refer this case for contempt, and the colloquy that you're having with Judge Rao seems to ignore the fact that there's evidence in the record that, as Judge Millett pointed out, there was a government official who said that we should say 'f you' to the courts and not obey court orders."
U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, jumped in before Shumate could answer.
"I don't think the district court here has suggested he is searching for additional contemners," Rao said, prompting Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Sri Srinivasan to tell Shumate to answer Pan's question.
Shumate repeated that Boasberg can "identify a specific person, and then issue the referral," and that's it.
"You agree that the notice has to include the person and the essential facts?" Pan followed up, pointing out that the reason Boasberg ordered additional testimony was the "extremely limited" nature of the government's representations.
"The Noem declaration had maybe two sentences in it," she observed.
The DOJ attorney dug in, and U.S. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard, another Obama appointee, seized on the U.S. government's "remarkable position" to essentially throw a cabinet secretary under the bus without any additional fact-finding about her state of mind.
"Part of why I say this is this is really a remarkable position is because you're suggesting the district court should refer for criminal prosecution a secretary, a secretary of homeland security, without any reason to think that she, in particular, was willful," Pillard said.
"I don't take lightly the fact that making a criminal referral is a serious step, but the district court in this case has indicated he's willing to do that and he has all the information to do that," the DOJ attorney repeated, emphasizing that the U.S. Supreme Court eventually vacated Boasberg's TRO.
Like several of her colleagues, Pillard indicated that Boasberg doesn't have "all the information" he needs because in order for there to be a contempt referral "it's the requirement is that there be a knowledge of the order and violation of it."
In the same vein, U.S. Circuit Judge J. Michelle Childs, a Biden appointee once championed by the late Lindsey Graham , commented on the potential unfairness of making Noem the "sacrificial lamb."
"Continuing to suggest here, 'district court, just take my word at it that this is the person,' That's also unfair to that alleged contemner who might be a sacrificial lamb," she said.

articles.content_orig:
The redesigned browser brings back compact mode and adds a theme picker.
Firefox is now looking quite different for most users after Mozilla started rolling out a redesign to everyone across desktop and mobile. The new look may not be too much of a surprise for some, though. Beta testers have been able to check it out through the Nightly version of the browser for the last few months.
Mozilla says it updated Firefox's themes, icons and colors to modernize it in line with features it has added recently, such as a single off switch for generative AI tools . The redesign itself brings more features to Firefox, as well as the return of compact mode, a much-requested option that Mozilla previously nixed. This minimizes how much screen real estate that the toolbar and tabs take up, so you can see more of the website. There's also a theme picker that includes wallpaper options and the ability to organize shortcuts on the New Tab screen.
Privacy settings are said to be easier to find , and Mozilla claimed it hasn't sacrificed performance. It added that the new Firefox doesn't place features like tab groups, split view and vertical tabs front and center, but they're still close at hand for those who want swift access. Moreover, Mozilla said it designed the customization options with accessibility in mind.

The focus of OpenAI’s Dev Day on Tuesday may have been on its agentic assistants known as Dots , or its new AI models , but combined, the AI company’s announcements pointed towards a bigger plan: a disruption of the traditional app store model. Taken together, today’s announcements turn ChatGPT itself into the place where software can be discovered, launched, and used by people and agents alike.
In addition, OpenAI introduced a way for people to bring their ChatGPT identity with them, while also allowing them to use their existing AI allowance in third-party apps.
This isn’t the first time OpenAI has experimented with how apps could operate within its familiar chatbot interface, but the current vision feels more fleshed out than before.
For starters, the company is turning ChatGPT itself into a surface for launching apps. The chatbot, which the company says now has 1.2 billion weekly users, has yet to fully capitalize on its potential as a discovery mechanism for finding and using apps that work with AI.
To change that, ChatGPT will begin to make app suggestions within the flow of conversation when it recognizes that a particular app could help the user complete their task. From there, the user will be able to connect the app and begin using it directly within ChatGPT.
This is also aided by the expansion of ChatGPT’s plugin architecture, which now supports extensions.
This allows app developers to build interactive panels where users can work with their tools while they’re chatting with ChatGPT. This essentially turns the apps and services that users would have previously used via the web or through a native desktop or mobile app into something that’s operated directly within ChatGPT.
Developers that sign on with the system can build AI-native versions of their apps through ChatGPT, the same way they would through the open web or a mobile app store. As more and more discovery happens through AI chat, it’s a distribution channel that’s hard to pass up.
Users get an incentive to use that channel too, because “ Sign in with ChatGPT ” will let them bring their AI allowance with them. (OpenAI has 16 launch partners on this effort, including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, but plans to add more soon, it says.)
In a demo at OpenAI’s Dev Day event, the company showed off how its own new meeting app could work inside ChatGPT, showing upcoming meetings from the user’s calendar. Here, the user could easily choose to use AI to take meeting notes, then receive a summary of follow-up items when the meeting wrapped.
In another example, users would work with design-focused apps like those from Figma and Adobe to work on revisions of their current project or use a particular feature that would have otherwise required a standalone app.
The apps can be shared with others, like work colleagues, in the lightweight websites ChatGPT now produces. From these ChatGPT sites, a user’s coworkers could sign in to the app with their own credentials and permissions, making the software experience personalized to them.
OpenAI also talked about improvements to how developers submit plugins for review — OpenAI’s version of Apple’s App Review process, if you will. Now, developers will be able to track their review, see what needs to be fixed, request a human review, and update their plugin’s tools without starting their whole submission over.
The company also announced a new enterprise app marketplace where partners can market their services. At launch, there are some 30-plus partners offering their app through the OpenAI Marketplace, including Adobe, Figma, Sierra, Decagon, HubSpot, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Harvey, Legora, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Baseten, and others. Eligible customers can apply part of their OpenAI commitment toward approved partner software, OpenAI said.
Beyond turning ChatGPT into an app discovery tool where users connect with apps directly, OpenAI’s embrace of agents is gently pushing users into a new era where they don’t have to think as much about which app to use or why, relying instead on their AI agents’ suggestions.
With the launch of its autonomous AI agents known as Dots , agents will navigate the web for you, executing the tasks that need to be done in their own cloud infrastructure. Each Dot has its own cloud computer and browser, and can also use connected apps. Compare this to the old model, where users who wanted to manage some type of project — like building a website or coordinating a meeting calendar — would have to download different apps to their computer or phone to make that happen.
Now, users will instead tell an AI agent what they want to have done, and it will simply do it for them. In some cases, the agent’s work may require access to another AI model or a particular application. But this is something the agent may bring to the user, rather than the other way around — where the user is the one to go out and seek the particular tool for the job.
As OpenAI explains, the Dots will be able to connect to its ecosystem of now over 4,000 apps.
What’s more, the Dots can be proactive, perhaps jumping in to offer help with a project or bug, or handling a task the user forgot — but all done with the user’s approval. The Dots will perform what OpenAI calls “proactive research” in the background using connected apps in a read-only mode, but users would still have control over the actions they take.
This system could give app makers another way to reach customers outside of Apple and Google’s app stores. For instance, users could subscribe to a service through the app maker’s website, then connect that account to ChatGPT or Codex for their agent to use. OpenAI has not said, however, that these features would eliminate the need for separate third-party subscriptions or other charges.
Notably, OpenAI didn’t tease any plans on this front today, instead focusing on how it’s building the discovery, distribution, and interface pieces to counter the app store model, along with an identity layer and a mechanism for sharing a user’s existing ChatGPT AI allowance. It did not announce plans Tuesday for a billing or revenue-sharing system that’s comparable to the economic layer of traditional app stores.

Six Flags Magic Mountain has permanently closed its X2 roller coaster after a series of lawsuits alleged that riders suffered severe brain injuries on the California attraction.
The Valencia theme park announced Tuesday that it had decided to retire the ride after nearly 20 years.
The ride, which Six Flags once called “a rite of passage for the ultimate daredevil,” reached 76 mph and 200 feet, with 3,610 feet of track, but has been closed since July 12 after two riders suffered life-threatening brain injuries less than a week apart.
“While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding said in a statement posted to the park’s website.
“Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously,” he added.
The coaster opened as X in 2002 and was redesigned with lighter trains before reopening as X2 in 2008. Its seats rotate 360 degrees as riders navigate drops, twists and inversions. Over 16 million people have ridden X2 since its 2008 reopening, Six Flags said.
However, more than 100 people allege that the two-minute, 34-second ride caused lasting brain injuries, according to a CNN investigation published last week.
Six Flags faces multiple lawsuits over the alleged injuries. CNN identified more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations associated with X2 over nearly two decades, including two deaths . Two riders suffered brain hemorrhages after riding the coaster in July, CNN reported.
Among the three most recent cases is Pamela Guillen, who visited Magic Mountain with her family in July to celebrate her daughter's 16th birthday. Guillen said she became confused and disoriented after riding X2 and later woke up in a hospital, where she learned she had suffered a traumatic brain injury and undergone emergency surgery.
“Everything went blank. My next memory is waking up in the hospital about two weeks later,” Guillen told ABC7 Los Angeles .
"I had suffered a traumatic brain injury and needed emergency brain surgery to stop the bleeding and had to be intubated. I was in a coma. I spent almost a month at the hospital," Guillen said.
Six days later, Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, 25, rode X2 and lost consciousness shortly afterward, according to her family's attorneys. She was taken to a hospital and underwent emergency brain surgery. Her family said she remained hospitalized and was unable to breathe on her own as of ABC7 Los Angeles ’ report last week.
A third recent plaintiff, Michael Wick, also alleges he suffered a brain injury after riding X2. His attorney said Wick underwent two brain surgeries and is now unable to practice law because of a disability.
The recent lawsuits follow the 2022 death of Christopher Hawley , 22, who lost consciousness shortly after getting off X2 and died the following day after suffering severe brain bleeding, according to his family's lawsuit.
His parents sued Six Flags, Magic Mountain and S&S Worldwide, the company associated with the ride's trains. The family reached a settlement in August, according to KTLA .
Hilda Farias, 28, also died after riding X2 in 2010, according to court records cited by the Los Angeles Times . She developed a brain bleed that led to her death.
Six Flags has declined multiple outlets’ requests for comment, citing pending litigation.
The Independent has contacted Six Flags for comment.
The X2 closure comes as Magic Mountain prepares to open Thrill Glider in 2027. Six Flags describes it as the world’s first suspended, multi-launch Thrill Glider coaster, featuring bike-like seats, five inversions, multiple launches and speeds of up to 50 mph.

articles.title_orig: What Jack Smith plans to tell the Senate Judiciary Committee
articles.title_zh: What Jack Smith plans to tell the Senate Judiciary Committee
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Former special counsel Jack Smith told senators Tuesday that he would not be silenced “by continued threats of prosecution” over his handling of the investigation into President Donald Trump.
Smith appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee amid the Justice Department’s push to target law enforcement officials involved with his investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol , as well as the probe into his handling of classified documents after he left office in January 2021.
Smith, who brought two since-dismissed federal criminal cases against Trump, said in his opening statement that he stood by his decision to bring charges against Trump, which was the result of a deep investigation that uncovered substantive evidence.
“The status, power, prominence, or political affiliation of the subject of an investigation must play no role in the decision to investigate, prosecute, or decline to prosecute,” he said.
“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation,” he said. Trump has said he did nothing wrong.
The hearing quickly devolved into a battleground of insults.
Louisiana Republican John Kennedy began his questioning by asking Smith: “What does the word arrogant mean?” And he ended his time by telling Smith: “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.”
Later, Missouri Republican Eric Schmitt called Smith a “dirtbag.”
The epithet came after Schmitt tried to imply that the former special counsel had been in communication with Fani Willis, the district attorney of Fulton County who was at the time working on a state case against Trump. Schmitt tried to place Smith in Atlanta at a Hawks game. When Smith denied it, Schmitt suggested he’d committed perjury.
But Schmitt appeared to have confused his basketball teams: Smith had actually been in attendance at an Iowa Hawkeyes game, which was Caitlin Clark’s team at the time.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., said Schmitt owed Smith an apology. He didn’t give it.
Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, has repeatedly criticized Smith. Grassley asserted that Smith misused his investigative powers and politically targeted Republicans. Smith, who as a career prosecutor went after Republicans and Democrats, has denied such allegations.
Grassley said that Smith must answer for what the senator portrays as “rampant abuse of authority and political targeting” funded by American taxpayers. He said his goal is to expose the “weaponization” of the Justice Department for actions taken during the Biden administration.
“Jack Smith’s corrupt operation undermined the rule of law and threatened our very political institutions,” he said Tuesday.
Smith has said he believes a jury would have convicted Trump in the 2020 election-related case had it gone to trial and that the notion that his decisions were “ influenced or directed by the Biden administration or other political actors is, in a word, laughable .” Smith’s final report in the election interference case stated that Trump “ inspired his supporters to commit acts of physical violence ” at the Capitol on Jan. 6.
Trump pleaded not guilty in Smith’s Jan. 6 case and denied after the attack that he incited his supporters, calling his remarks at a rally that day “totally appropriate.” Trump later described Jan. 6 defendants as “hostages” and gave them mass clemency upon his return to office.
The Trump administration last year launched a so-called grand conspiracy investigation looking at actions taken by federal law enforcement officials dating back to 2016, which would fall outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes .
The Trump administration also has purged FBI and Justice Department officials involved in past Trump investigations. Defense attorneys for current and former officials informed a court last week that DOJ officials appear interested in probing the circumstances of an August 2022 FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, during which agents found classified documents that were at the heart of one of the since-dismissed Trump cases.
Joe diGenova, who was a federal prosecutor during Ronald Reagan’s presidency, headed up the “grand conspiracy” investigation until he left the Justice Department this month. He told NBC News that “ lanes got crossed ” in his final days.
Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said the law enforcement who worked diligently on the cases were fired for doing their jobs, then vilified  and harassed by Trump and his allies who are still “pushing false narratives that somehow Donald Trump is the victim.”
“This is an eight-year attempt to lie to the American people, and this is their closing argument, everybody, right before an election, this is what they want to spend their time on: perpetrating a lie,” Booker said.
In his first public testimony before Congress earlier this year, Smith told the House Judiciary Committee that he would not be intimidated and predicted that the Trump administration would attempt to launch a criminal case against him. Months later, one of Trump’s allies on Capitol Hill, Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, asked the Trump administration to investigate Jordan’s assertion that Smith “seemingly” made false statements in congressional testimony.
Smith’s lawyers said he provided “truthful, responsive answers” and that Jordan’s referral “reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.” Former federal prosecutors have told NBC News that the Justice Department would have a tough time bringing a perjury case against Smith.
Smith didn’t discuss the classified documents investigation because Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon ordered that that portion of his report as special counsel cannot be released. The Justice Department has taken the position that answering questions about that investigation would violate Cannon’s order.

articles.title_orig: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.title_zh: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.content_orig:
Are panda’s ursine politicians? Well, actually, they’re more like international statesmen.
And some Northeastern University experts believe that a pair of Chinese giant pandas that arrived in the U.S. on Sunday are a sign of soothing tensions between Beijing and Washington.
“Pandas are an unusually effective diplomatic symbol,” said Xiaoxiao Shen , an assistant research professor at Northeastern who focuses on Chinese international politics.
“They are associated with China but aren’t controversial.”
It’s called “soft diplomacy”, said Daniel Aldrich , a Northeastern University professor who teaches political science, describing a diplomatic tool used to show good will to other nations.
Typically it is done by giving food, medicine, other aid – or in this case, pandas –  to help inspire people in foreign countries to feel more favorable to your nation, he said.
“China wants to see happy headlines about pandas and not the abuse of the Uyghurs,” a minority population in China, Aldrich said.
Shen explained that as political tensions rise and fall between the U.S. and China, pandas are given or taken away. There used to be 20 Chinese-owned pandas at American zoos. Since 2024, all but six have gone home, as relations between Beijing and Washington have ebbed and flowed.
“There is a clear political dimension,” Shen said.
The arrival of the pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, at  Zoo Atlanta after their 8,000 mile journey from Chengdu, China, was announced by Chinese president Xi Jinping as he stood beside President Trump at a visit to the White House on Sept. 24.
Xi declared that the bears were an “envoy of friendship.”
The practice of giving bears dates back to the Tang dynasty in the early about 1,500 years ago, at a time when daughters were often given in marriage to foreign kings and nomadic rulers in China to solidify treaties and border disputes, said Mark Henderson , a Northeastern political science professor who teaches at the Oakland campus.
The Bronx zoo received two pandas from China in 1941 and in 1972 the People’s Republic of China gifted then President Richard Nixon and his wife Pat with a pair of pandas, Hsing-Hsing and Ling-Ling, as a gesture of friendship.
Aside from deploying bears as a goodwill gesture, China has been using soft diplomacy to gain favor elsewhere in the world, including in Africa where it has launched vaccination programs and invested heavily in building roads, bridges, ports and other infrastructure, Aldrich said.
A July 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 36 nations found that China is seen more favorably than the U.S. across the globe with countries expressing more confidence in Xi than Trump. Even America’s closest neighbors Canada and Mexico – view China more positively than the U.S., the nonprofit thinktank found.
“There are two ways to influence people around the world,” Aldrich said. “The first is to bomb them. The second is to feed them, give them aid. As we’ve seen in Iran over these last seven months, bombs aren’t working.”
The U.S. had used soft diplomacy to great success in past years. In 1948, America  committed $15 billion to the Marshall Plan to help rebuild Western Europe following World War II. The approach built trust and strong alliances as “America [was] is seen as the friendly nation,” Aldrich said.
But in recent years, the U.S. has all but dismantled the United States Agency for International Development or USAID, a state-run program that in 2023 spent about $40 billion in food, medical and emergency assistance across the globe according to the Congressional Research Service, according to Pew. That aid ended in 2025 when the government functionally dismantled the program.
In addition, the U.S. also cut ties with the World Health Organization, or WHO, in 2025, citing mismanagement and lack of transparency, according to a release from the U.S. Health and Human Services Department.
“People around the world, especially Africa, think that America has abandoned them,” Henderson said, as the lion’s share of USAID went to nations on that continent.
But the pandas coming-to-America moment is a sign of political thawing between the U.S. and China – at least for now, experts said.
“The pandas are given or taken away as China thinks favorably of you or not,” Henderson said.
